title: The Amplification of Exaggerated and False News on Social Media: The Roles of Platform Use, Motivations, Affect, and Ideology
screen_reason: Nationally representative UK survey (n = 2,005 social media users) that reports the share of respondents who self-report having shared exaggerated or false news in the past month without correcting it: 33.8% of the 589 political-news sharers, which the authors state is 9.9% of all UK social media users. This is a share of survey respondents reporting SHARING misinformation, i.e. RECALL (sharing subtype), with an explicit denominator.

estimates.platform: social media in general (respondents screened as users of Facebook, Twitter, Instagram or WhatsApp; sharing question worded 'share news on social media')
estimates.measure_type: % of UK social media users who report having shared exaggerated or false news in the past month without correcting it (amplification)
estimates.value_raw: 9.9% of all UK social media users (a tenth); equivalently 33.8% of the 589 past-month political-news sharers among 2,005 social media users
estimates.denominator: 2,005 UK social media users (Opinium Research online panel, quota sampling on age, gender and region; participation rate 32.8%); respondents who never use Facebook, Twitter, Instagram or WhatsApp were screened out
estimates.definition: Respondent recalled sharing, in the past month, a news story that was made up or exaggerated (any of the four scale points) AND, on the follow-up probe, said they 'shared the news as it was, without correcting it' rather than providing information to correct inaccuracies
estimates.misinfo_def: "we focus on the amplification of false or misleading information, which we define as the sharing of exaggerated or false news without seeking to correct inaccuracies in the news"
estimates.source_quote: As Table 1 shows, a third (33.8%) of UK social media users who shared news in the past month amplified exaggerated or false news (RQ1). This amounts to a tenth (9.9%) of all UK social media users
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report with one-month recall; amplification separated from corrective sharing by a follow-up item ('did you provide information to correct inaccuracies in it, or did you simply share the news as it was?'), with correctors recoded to zero; authors note the measure presupposes accurate recall and awareness of falsity and therefore likely under-estimates prevalence
estimates.moderator_quote: "Respondents who said they never use at least one of the four most popular digital media platforms in the UK (Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and WhatsApp) were immediately screened out of the survey, leaving an overall sample size of 2,005 social media users."
estimates.notes: Headline row: 9.9% is stated verbatim in the results text, so it is kept even though it is arithmetically 33.8% of the 589/2,005 sharer subgroup. platform_norm coded 'survey' because the instrument asks about social media in general with no platform breakdown of the outcome (the four platforms appear only as predictors); 'multi_platform' is the defensible alternative. Only the 589 respondents who had shared political news at least once in the past month were asked the amplification questions, so the 2,005 denominator treats non-sharers (and the 102 missing) as non-amplifiers.

Flagged definition_variant=true purely as a do-not-double-count marker; strictly this is a denominator variant, not a stricter/broader definition of misinformation. 33.8% is printed verbatim in the text, so it is not a complement I computed from Table 1's 66.2%.

estimates.measure_type: % of past-month political-news sharers who report knowingly sharing news they thought was made up when they shared it, without correcting it
estimates.value_raw: 7.6% of sharers; Table 1: '4. You thought was made up when you shared it 45 7.6' of n = 589
estimates.denominator: 589 respondents (of 2,005 UK social media users) who reported sharing political news on social media at least once in the past month
estimates.definition: Respondent selected the most problematic scale point - shared a news story they 'thought was made up when [they] shared it' - and did not provide information to correct inaccuracies

estimates.source_quote: However, the more problematic behavior was also evident: 7.6% of sharers said they knowingly amplified made-up news.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report; respondents selecting more than one option were placed at the most problematic point on the scale
estimates.moderator_quote: "Following Chadwick et al. (2018), if a respondent selected more than one option, they were placed at the point on the scale for the most problematic sharing behavior."
estimates.notes: Strictest definition variant of the headline measure: deliberate sharing of fabricated news. 7.6% is verbatim in the text and matches Table 1 (45/589 = 7.64%).

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Table 1's other individual scale points are printed as percentages of the 589 sharers - '1. Seemed accurate at the time, but you later found out was made-up 52 8.8', '2. Was exaggerated, and you were not aware of this 87 14.8' (also stated verbatim in the text as 14.8%), '3. Was exaggerated, and you were aware of this 15 2.5'. I did not create rows for these because they are mutually exclusive categories of one ordinal scale, not cumulative prevalences; a reader would misread any one of them as 'the' prevalence, and combining them into e.g. 'any made-up news' (8.8 + 7.6) would be a cross-category sum barred by R8. The cumulative figure the paper itself reports (33.8% / 9.9%) is extracted instead. 2) '29.4% (589) shared political news at least once in the past month' - a share of news sharers, not of misinformation, so no row. 3) 'Exposure to inaccurate political news on social media in the past month' was measured as a control variable but its descriptive distribution is only in the (unavailable) Supplemental Appendix Table A1a - a likely RECALL-exposure estimate that this text does not carry. 4) All other numbers in Table 2 are odds ratios from an ordered logistic regression, not prevalences.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey of a UK national panel (Opinium Research), fielded 5-16 July 2018; random sampling of panel recruits with quotas for age, gender and region of residence; participation rate 32.8%; median completion 9 minutes; n = 2,005 after screening out non-users of Facebook/Twitter/Instagram/WhatsApp. Only the 589 respondents who reported sharing political news in the past month were asked the amplification battery. Outcome is a rank-ordered 0-4 self-report scale, with a follow-up probe recoding corrective sharers to zero. Missing values on independent/control variables were multiply imputed (five datasets) for the regression only. Authors flag social-desirability bias and recall error as likely sources of UNDER-estimation. No inter-coder reliability applies (self-report instrument).
rob.item6_quote: Sometimes people might share news on social media that turns out not to be fully accurate or is exaggerated. In the past month, do you recall sharing a news story that. . ." Respondents could choose from: "seemed accurate at the time, but you later found was made up" (scored 1); "was exaggerated, and you were not aware of this" (scored 2); "was exaggerated, and you were aware of this" (scored 3); "you thought was made up when you shared it" (scored 4); or "none of the above" (scored zero).
